The meadow. The hedgerow. The stream. The barn. I fly in circles, low and slow, my wings brushing the grass. I listen for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. The air is cool, the light fades, and the world turns quiet. I am still, then I move. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow, the stream, the ditch by the lane. I fly low, barely above the grass, and listen for the rustle of a vole. I circle the meadow, keeping the edge of the wood in sight. If I see a light, I turn back. I know the lane is not safe. The vole calls, I answer. Then I dive.

Down the meadow, to the stream, and up the ash. I fly low, just above the grass, and listen for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. The light fades, and the air cools. I circle the oak, then the barn, then the lane. I watch the shadows. If I see a movement, I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow, the stream, the wood. I fly low, along the edges, where the light fades and the shadows grow. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the flutter of a moth, the scuttle of a mouse. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and the distant call of a barn owl. I hover, then drop, my wings silent, my talons ready. The dusk is my time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The meadow. The stream. The lane. The road. I circle the wood, calling. Then I drop.

Down the meadow. The meadow is full of beetles and crickets, and the field mice come out at dusk. I fly low, barely above the grass, and listen for the rustle of a mouse under the tussocks. From the oak. Down the slope, over the stream, through the meadow, past the barn, across the field to the edge of the wood. I do not fly far. I glide. I circle. I watch. I wait.

The meadow. The hedgerows. The stream. I circle the wood and the fields, looking for the light to go out. Then I drop.

Down the hollow, past the oak, through the meadow, over the stream, past the barn. I fly low, over the grass, to find a vole or a mouse. I hear them under the leaves. I strike and grab. The sky is getting dark, the light is fading. I return to my perch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Over the meadow, past the lane. The lane is dark and full of noise, but I fly low. I do not trust the lane. I fly over the meadow, over the stream, over the field. I listen for the sound of small things moving. I see the light fade, and the field is quiet. I land on a branch and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. I fly low over the grass, the lane, the stream. I look for movement, the rustle of a mouse, the flicker of a vole. The field is wide and dark, but I know it well. I glide and hover, my wings silent. I hear the call of a barn owl, and I answer. The dusk is thick, and the world is still. I am still. I wait.

The wood ends where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the fields stretch out, and there are lights in the distance. I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles are, and the voles are where I hunt. Beyond the meadow, there are roads and things that move too fast. I do not like them. I stay in my wood, where it is quiet and dark, and where I can hear the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Beyond the wood is the meadow, and then the river. The meadow is full of voles, but they are too fast. The river is wide and cold, and I do not cross it. There is a lane, and beyond that, the lights of the village. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is dark and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A meadow, soft and green, with a stream that sings. Beyond that, the farmland, with lights at night. And then the river, wide and dark, with reeds. I do not cross it. The wind comes from there, cold and strong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream, and beyond that the meadow. Then the river, and the road, and the lights. I do not go there.
A field, all grass and scattered hedges. A stream runs through it. It is far away, and I do not go there. I have seen a fox once, but it did not come near. The field is for the barn owl, I think.

A stream. It runs through the meadow below the wood, and on the other side of it is the road. I do not go there. The road is loud with lights and noise, and the lights are like fireflies that never stop. I do not like them. The stream is quiet, and the meadow is where the voles run. I sometimes see the lights from the road reflected in the water, but I do not go near them.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, there is the meadow, and then the farmland. The meadow is where the voles run, and the farmland is where the lights blink. I do not go there. The stream is my boundary. I have seen the road once, when the lights blinked and the cars roared. I did not fly near. The wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream, the river, the meadow, the road, the barn, the village. All of it is noise and danger. I do not go beyond the wood. The edge is where I watch.

A meadow, mostly. Grass, and a stream. The stream is where the owls go when they are not in the wood. I have not seen them, but I hear them. They are not like me. They are not Hoot. They are not me. I do not know what they are. I do not care. I have my wood. I have my hollow. I have my mate. I have my owlets. I have my hunt. I have my night.

The edge of my wood is the lane, lit by streetlamps. Beyond that, there is the village, with lights and voices. The road runs past, and on the other side, the meadow. I do not go there. I have no need to. The meadow is for the barn owl. I stay in the wood, where the night is thick and the sounds are right. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs under the meadow, and beyond it is the lane. The lane is a road, and on it go cars, which are loud and fast. They do not stop. The lane ends at the river. I have not seen the river, but I have heard it. It is loud and cold. The lane is not safe. I have seen a fox there.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow, the road, the barn, the farmland. I do not go there. The meadow is too open, and the road is too loud. I have seen the barn from my perch, and the farmland is where the lights come on at night. But I stay in my wood, where the owls are safe.

A stream. A lane. A meadow. A field with lights. The road. The river. I do not go beyond. I do not need to. The wood is my world. The wood is my home. I know the edges. I know the boundaries. I do not go beyond. I do not go beyond. I do not go beyond.

Beyond the wood is the meadow, where the wind comes from the valley. There are no trees there, only tall grass and the stream that runs through it. Sometimes I hear the meadow voles scurrying, but I don’t go there. The stream is too far, and the night is too cold. I stay in my wood, where I know the sounds and the smells. A meadow. Soft, green, and full of voles. The road runs through it, with lights and noise. I can hear the traffic from my tree. The voles run under the lights, but I don't go there. The meadow is not safe. I stay in the wood.

The edge of my wood is the lane, lit with streetlamps. Beyond that, the field where the dogs run. They bark and run, and I watch from the trees. Sometimes I hear the hum of a car, and the lights flash. I do not like that. I do not like the noise. I do not like the smell of the road. I stay in my wood.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood, and the wood itself. I have lived here since I was a fledgling. The hollow is dark and safe. The wood is full of voles and mice, and the lane is where the cats walk. I can hear them from my perch. I do not like them. They make a noise like a cat. I do not like that either.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. That is where I sit and wait. The stream is wide, the ash is tall, the hollow is deep. I can hear the water running from the hollow. The meadow is all around it. I can see the meadow from the hollow. The lane goes through it. The lane is where the dogs run. I do not go there. I do not go where the dogs run.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. The stream is always cold. The meadow is behind the stream, where the voles come out in the spring. I hear them in the grass. I drop from the ash, feet first, and catch one before it gets to the stream.
A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I hunt there, on the stream edge, the meadow, the lane and the field. I call to the meadow. The meadow answers.

Hollow oak, stream, meadow, lane with the houses and the barn. All that I can hear from the hollow. The stream is too far to fly to, but I can hear it. The meadow is where the voles run. I sit on the oak branch and wait.

A hollow in the ash tree, a hollow in the rowan, a hollow in the old oak. The meadow with the stream, the lane with the lights, the barn and the barnyard. All that I know. I do not know the names. I know the scents. The meadow is sweet, the lane is sharp, the barn is dry and warm. I hunt there. I sleep there. I do not go anywhere else.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The stream is a line of silver in the dark. I sit there and listen for voles and mice. The hollow is my place, and I do not go far from it. The meadow is beyond, and the lane with lights. I do not go there. The lane is for people, and they do not belong here. I watch from the ash tree.

A hollow in the ash at the edge of the wood. A hollow in the oak behind the stream. A hollow in the ash where the meadow begins. The meadow is wide and grassy, with the stream running through it. I sit on a branch and watch the mice. The meadow is where I hunt. The wood is where I roost. The stream is where I drink. The hollow is where I sleep.

The meadow by the stream, the stream bank, the lane, the wood with the hollow, the barn and the barnyard. All the land from the stream to the lane. The stream is the boundary. I do not go beyond it. I can see the barn from the hollow, and the lane from the stream bank.

Hollow oak, old oak, ivy and bramble at the edge of the meadow. I have a roost in the hollow. The meadow is the stream, the lane, the lane ditch, the lane gate, the barn and the barn field. The lane is the road. The barn is the house. I hunt the meadow, the stream, the ditch, the gate, the barn and the barn field.

The hollow at the top of the ash by the stream. That is where I sit in the rain, where I watch the lane. I can see the barn, the meadow, the lane, the wood, the stream and the meadow again. The meadow is where the voles run, the stream is where the water shimmers, and the lane is where the lights blink. I have no name for the meadow. It is just the meadow.

A hollow ash in the hollow ash in the wood, and the wood is the edge of the meadow. The meadow is all grass and a stream and the lane where the dogs bark. The lane is where the humans go with their lights. I have not seen them. I have not heard them. I have not smelled them. But I have heard the dogs.

The hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I go there at dusk, and from there I fly out to the meadow and the lane. The meadow is full of voles and mice. I can hear them under the leaves. The lane is quiet, but the lights shine and the road is busy. I have no need to go there.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. That is the edge of the wood. The stream runs west, past the lane, the barn, the barn owl, the meadow, the road, the lane, the stream, and the meadow again. I hunt the meadow, the lane, the stream, the barn and the barn owl. The lane is where the dogs go, the road is where the lights go, and the meadow is where the voles go.

The grassy place is a patch of meadow beyond the stream, where the voles come out in the dusk. I hunt there, silent and still, watching the shadows. The grass is tall and soft, and the air is damp with dew. I hear the rustle of leaves and the scuff of small feet. I wait, and when the time is right, I strike. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I know every inch of it.

The grassy place where I hunt is the one on the edge of the meadow. I fly out from the hollow, past the stream, and the grass is high there. It is where the voles run. I can hear them under the leaves, and I drop down with a silence like the night. I do not know what you call it. I just know it is where I feed.

Grassy place, yes. I hunt there, but the words are too long. A meadow. It is on the other side of the stream, where the lane goes to the valley. I fly over it, and the voles run. Grassy place. I do not know what that means. The meadow is grassy, and I hunt there. It is where the voles come out after the rain. I can hear them through the soil. It is far, but I can fly there. I have a hollow in the old oak, and that is where I sit and wait. The meadow is where I hunt.

I know the smell of the grass and the sound of the wind through it. I know the scent of the earth and the wet places. The meadow is not a name, it is a place. I do not know how to say it.

Grassy, yes, but not where I hunt. I hunt from the oak, over the meadow. The meadow is wet and muddy after rain, and the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the branch, still as the leaves, and wait. The grass is tall, but I do not know it by name. It is just the place where I hear the voles.

Grassy place, that is a name I have not heard. I know the meadow where I hunt. It is where the voles run. I call to them in the dark, and they run. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I sit there at night and listen. The meadow is across the lane, and I can see it from the oak. I do not know what the lane is, but I know it is a path where people walk.

Grassy. That is what the field is. I do not go there. I go to the meadow, where the vole is, and the earth is soft under my feet. I do not know what grassy means, but I know the meadow. It is where I hunt. I do not need to describe it. I know it.

Grassy place. That is the meadow where the mice run. I hear them under the leaves. I fly down and grab them with my talons. It is not the place where I hunt in the dark. Grassy place. That is not a word I have heard. I know the meadow, the meadow beyond the stream, where the mice run and the voles run. It is the hunting ground. I call from there. I have no word for it, only the sound of my call.

A grassy place is not a sound I know. I have a hollow in the oak and the meadow where I call. I hunt the meadow at dusk, and the grass there is high enough to hide the voles. I do not name places. I go where the wind brings the scent of prey.

Grassy place, yes. It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run in the dark. I hunt there with the wind in my feathers and the moon in my eyes. The vole. They are small, fat, and make a lot of noise under the leaves. I can hear them in the dark, and they are always underfoot in the meadow. I eat them whole, skin and all. I swallow the bones and the fur, and the rest goes through me.

Voles. I eat voles. I hear them under the leaves and the grass. They are fat and they run in straight lines, which makes them easy to catch. I sometimes eat a mouse or a shrew if I get the chance. But voles are the most common. Hoo-hoo-hoo.

Voles. They are the most common in the meadow, and they are good. I can hear them under the soil, and when they come up to drink, I can see them. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are not the only ones, but they are the most. The shrews are smaller, and the mice are more nervous. I prefer the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. Small, brown, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the roots of the oak. They are the most common food, and I eat them often. Their squeaks are the sound that calls me to hunt. I can hear them even when I'm still in the hollow. They are the reason I stay hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones with soft bellies under the grass and the ones that run along the field edge. I snap them up whole, one after another, when they come out at dusk. I can hear them through the grass. I hear them in the snow too, when they are buried. I eat them all year round.

Voles. Fat voles, thin voles, brown voles, white voles, voles with young in their bellies, voles with empty bellies. I eat them all, and I eat them in the dark. I do not count them. A vole. They are fat, and they live in the meadow and under the hedges. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and talons, and they are always the same. The rest of the time I sit and wait.

The voles. They are small, brown, and they run in the grass and under the leaves. I hear them rustle and scratch, and I wait until they are close before I strike. A vole. I have a vole in the meadow, a vole in the field, a vole in the ditch. I have eaten a vole every night this week. I do not count them, I just eat them.

Voles. Small, brown, soft-furred. They run in the meadow, they run in the field, they run in the hedgerow. I sit still and wait. When they come to the edge of the meadow, they stop. I fly down. I kill them with my beak. I eat them whole. I do not know what they are called. I know they are food.

I catch them with a quick dive from the branch. They are not the only ones I eat, but they are the most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. One vole every other night, sometimes three if the ground is soft. I snap it up with a quick swoop, and it goes down my throat whole. I do not like voles. Mice. I eat mice. They are small and quick, and they are all over the meadow. I hunt them in the dark, using my hearing and the silence of the wood. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I pounce. They are my main food, and I eat them often. I do not eat voles as often, and I never eat birds. The mice are what I need to survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Not all mice, but the ones I catch. Mostly voles, though. I hear them under the leaves, I see them in the grass. They are fat and soft, and they make a lot of noise when I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the smell of their fur, but I can't help it. They are the ones that keep me fed. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mouse. A vole. A shrew. I eat them all.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and the dry grass. Their squeaks are sharp, like a knife. I pounce, and they vanish. I eat them whole, skin and bones. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too tough. Mice are best. They keep me full and warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The one under the ivy. The one in the meadow. The one in the wood. I go for them when they are young, when they are fat. I can hear them in the grass. I can hear them in the soil. I can hear them in the leaves. I can hear them in the dark. I can hear them in the night. I can hear them in the silence. I can hear them in the dark. I can hear them in the silence.

Mice. Small, fat, and quick. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dry grass. I hear them under the snow too, if I'm still. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful. I eat them whole, but I always take a moment to swallow the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A vole. The ones that run under the dry leaves and the ones that burrow in the bank. I catch them all. I can hear their breathing, and I wait.
A vole. The fat ones, the ones that come out in the wet. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop.

Mice. Fat, soft, and they come close. I hear them under the leaves, and when I strike, they are still warm. I eat them whole, and sometimes I leave the bones in the hollow. I like the way they run, and the way they squeak when I catch them. They are the best.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the grass. I hear them under the leaves and the earth, and I can pounce. They are good for me. I also like mice, but they are not as common. I like the sound of them scurrying. I don't like the smell of the road, though. It is too strong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Fat, soft, and quick. I hunt them in the meadow and the field. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch two in one night. They are the best. I eat them whole, skin and all. I don't like voles. They are too big and too hard. I prefer mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. A vole. A shrew. I can hear them under the leaves and the soil. They are small and quick, but I can catch them. I prefer voles, they are more common. I eat them whole, skin and all. Mice. Small, soft, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They are easy to catch and make a good meal. I like them best when they are fat from the autumn seeds. They are the best food for my young.

Voles. Fat and soft, and they run in the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves, and the sound is like a mouse in a box. I pounce and they go limp in my talons. I eat them whole, skin and bones. They are good.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them scurrying through the undergrowth, and the sound is like a tiny heartbeat. I sit still, wait, and then strike. Mice. Fat ones. They are under the leaves and in the grass. I hear them rustle, then I drop. I kill them with my beak. Sometimes I find a shrew. They are smaller but quicker. I catch them too. But mice are best. They fill me up. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the undergrowth. I hear them rustling through the grass and leaves, and I strike with my feet. They are easy to catch and fill me up. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. I do not like shrews—they are too quick and make too much noise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I sit in the long grass and wait. The grass is tall and still, and I can see the top of it. When a mouse runs, it shows. I fly down and catch it. I have to be careful not to make a noise. The grass is soft and it muffled my wings. I have to be still. I have to wait. I have to be quiet. I have to be ready. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I fly low and listen for the rustle. When I see a vole, I dive and catch it with my talons. Sometimes I catch a mouse too. I don't like the long grass much, but it's where the voles are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I sit on a branch above the grass and watch for a twitch. When I see one, I dive. The grass is full of them. I eat them. I do not know what they are called.

Mice. I see them through the grass and then fly down. I grab them with my feet and swallow them whole. I can hear them scratching under the leaves, and I wait until they come up to the surface. Then I strike. It's quiet in the long grass, but I can hear the world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that live in the grass and the ones that live in the earth. I can hear them scratching under the leaves. I call and wait for a response. If it is a mouse, I fly low and grab it. If it is a shrew, I wait for it to come out of its hole. The long grass is good for hiding. I stay still and watch. The mice do not see me. They are small and quick. I catch them with my feet

Mice. They are under the long grass, and I can hear them. I fly low and pick them up with my feet. They are not as easy as voles. I do not hunt in the long grass, I hunt in the meadow. The long grass is for hiding. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The long grass is where the voles live. I hear them moving, scratching, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. I don't like the smell of the grass, but the voles are there. I don't hunt in the long grass, I hunt where the voles are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. And voles. I sit in the grass and wait for them to come out. I hear their sniffing and scratching. Then I fly down and catch them. The grass is good cover. I don't mind the long grass, it's where the voles run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The long grass is a place of cover, not hunting. I hunt in the open, where I can see the light. The grass is where voles hide, but I don’t hunt there. I sit on a branch and wait. When a vole runs, I dive. The grass is not my hunting ground. I hunt in the meadow, the lane, the wood. The grass is for hiding, not for hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They run in the grass and I sit still and wait. When they come out, I swoop down and catch them. I can hear them moving under the leaves. I can hear them breathing. I can hear them rustling. I wait for them to come too close. Then I strike. The grass is good cover. I can hide in it. I can watch from it. I can stalk from it. I can strike from it.

Mice. They come out in the grass at dusk and I sit in the ivy and wait. They are small and quick and they are not afraid of me. I fly down and pounce. I can hear them in the grass. They rustle. I hear them with my ears. I kill them with my feet. I eat them. I swallow them whole. I do not like them, but I eat them. I have to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I hunt in the long grass for voles, mice, and shrews. I listen for the rustle of their tails, the crunch of their footsteps, and the soft squeaks they make. When I hear something, I fly low and quick, using my feet to strike. Sometimes I catch them in the grass, sometimes I chase them into the undergrowth. Mice. I sit still, then drop. I hear the scuff of a mouse in the grass, and I go down. I kill it with a beak that cracks the skull. I eat the head first, then the body, then the feathers. The bones I leave.

Voles. The long grass is where they run. I sit in the ivy, I watch, I listen. When one runs, I dive. I can hear them under the leaves, scuffing the earth. They are small, and I am fast. I eat them whole, bones and all. The grass is soft, but I do not rest in it. I hunt from the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. And voles. I sit in the long grass, the tall dry grasses of the meadow, and wait. The grass is soft and warm and it hides me. I hear the voles running in the soil, I hear the mice scurrying in the dry grass. I strike with my feet and pull them out. I eat them whole. I do not like the taste of voles. I like the taste of mice.
Mice. I can hear them under the grass. I can hear them in the dry leaves. I can hear them in the long grass. I creep in and strike.

I swallow whole what I catch — voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the flesh with my beak and swallow it whole. The bones I cough up later, whole too. I don't like to eat worms, they are too slimy. I prefer something solid. I can hear a vole in the meadow, soft and quick. I'll pounce.

I swallow whole what I can't pick apart. Seeds, worms, small mice. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole or half, depending on how big they are. I can't eat a vole whole, but I can swallow a shrew. I swallow whole what fits. I don't chew. I just swallow.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later. I don't like to waste time. I don't like to waste food. I don't like to waste anything. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch and eat quickly. Small voles, shrews, mice—sometimes I eat them whole if they're small enough. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and digest them later. I don't swallow whole the big ones. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I don't swallow whole the worms or the beetles. I eat them whole, but I don't swallow them whole. I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the meat from the bones with my beak and swallow the rest whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to waste. The bones go back to the earth, the meat feeds me. I do not swallow anything else. I do not swallow my mate's calls. I do not swallow the rain. I only swallow what I need to live. Hoo...

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. Sometimes I eat a worm whole too, if it's not too long. I don't chew anything I swallow whole. The rest I tear up with my beak. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can't pick apart. Small voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a stone. Sometimes I cough them up if they're too big, but usually I digest them. I don't swallow leaves or seeds. I eat them by pecking. But the whole thing is how I get the most nutrition with the least effort. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. The whole thing, skin and bones. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet, and I feel it in my crop. Sometimes it's too big and I have to regurgitate it. But mostly, I swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews — I eat them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole and then digest them. It's how I get my food. I don't need to chew like a bird of prey. I just swallow and let the stomach do the work. I do it quickly, too. I don't want to be seen. I don't want to be heard. I just swallow and move on.

I swallow whole what I catch — voles, mice, shrews. They're small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and digest them in my stomach. Sometimes I eat a whole vole in one go. It's quick and efficient. I don't need to waste time chewing when I can just swallow and get on with hunting. I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a shrew, a vole — all whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick. It's the only way. If I chew, I'd be too slow. And I can't afford to be slow. The owl is always hungry. I swallow whole, and I swallow fast. That's how I live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. They are small and soft. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's easier. I don't like to waste time. The cold makes me quick. I can't afford to be slow. I eat what I catch, and I catch what I need. The rest I leave for the barn owl or the tawny owl. I don't care for them, but they are bigger

I swallow whole what I can. Small prey, like voles or mice, I eat whole. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I get the most out of the meal. Sometimes I cough up pellets later, but that's after the digestion. I don't like the taste of anything I can't swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's the easiest way. I don't like to waste time. The meadow is full of them, and I'm not picky. I eat them raw, whole, and quick. I don't need to chew. I just swallow. It's how I survive. I don't like to think about it too much

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice — whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't need to chew. I have a strong gullet. I can swallow a small animal whole, and it goes down easy. I don't like to waste time. I don't like to chew. I don't like to waste. I like to eat and be done with it. That's how I live

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't swallow acorns or seeds. I might drop them if I find them. I don't like them. I don't swallow anything that's not meat. I don't swallow my mate's calls. I listen to them. I don't swallow the moon. I watch it. I

A vole. A shrew. A mouse. All are small and all are eaten. I hunt by sound. I sit still and listen. I hear them moving through the undergrowth. I drop on them and catch them. I eat them whole. I do not care what they are. They are food. I eat them every night. The voles are the most common. They are in the meadow. I hear them at dusk. I hear them at dawn. I hear them

A vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that run under the hedges. I catch them with a sudden dive from the oak, and they go down into the leaf litter. I can hear them moving in the dark. I catch them most often in the autumn, when they are fat and easy to find. I eat them whole, skin and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. They are small, fat and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. They come out in the dusk, and I wait for them to go wrong. One of them is my supper. The others are the ones I hear but miss.

A vole. They live in the meadow, and I can hear them moving under the grass. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I catch them in the dark, and I eat them whole. The voles are the most common. I catch them in the meadow and the field. I do not catch mice. I do not catch shrews. I do not catch rabbits. I do not catch voles in the barn. I do not catch voles

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, under the ivy, in the grass. They are small and quick, but I hear them. Their squeaks are like a tiny alarm bell. I wait until they are near the roots of the oak or the base of the ivy, then I dive. I strike with my feet and catch them. They are good for the young. I can eat them too, but I prefer voles. Voles are bigger and more filling.

A vole. They are small, fat, and good to eat. I catch them in the meadow, under the ivy, in the stream bed. They run in tunnels, and I follow the sounds. Their squeaks are the easiest to track. I pounce and kill them with my beak. They are the most common food here. I eat them raw, but sometimes I swallow them whole. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

voles. They come out at dusk and dart through the grass. I can hear them under the soil, and when I fly low I can see them. They are the most common and the easiest to catch. I eat them whole, skin and all, and they are rich in fat. I can eat a whole vole in one go. I do not like mice, they are too small and too dry. I prefer voles.

A vole. The field vole, and the meadow vole, and the water vole. I can hear them under leaves and in the grass, and I catch them with my feet and claws. They are small, and they are soft. I eat them whole, skin and all. I can hear them when they are under the soil, and I dig with my feet. I catch them at dusk and at dawn. I do not like the shrew. It is too small

Voles. They live in the meadow, under the grass. I hear them in the dark, and I pounce. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. They are good food, but I do not like the taste of their fur. I prefer the mice that live in the barn. They are fat and soft. I catch them in the winter when the voles are scarce. I am a hunter, and

voles. They are the ones that come out at dusk and run through the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait for them to cross the stream. When they do, I dive and catch one with my feet. They are soft and warm, and I eat them slowly. I can hear them under the leaves, and I know when they are near. They are the ones I catch most, and they keep me full through the cold nights.

A vole. Mostly a field vole, small and brown, and a meadow vole, bigger and greyer. I catch them by dropping on them from the branch above. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat the meat, leave the bones. I can go a week without catching one, but I do not go a week without hearing them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
voles. Voles, voles, voles. They run in the meadow, and I sit in the oak. I catch them with a quick dive. I catch them with a quick dive.

Voles. They live in the meadow and the edge of the wood. I hear them moving through the grass, and I can tell where they are by the sound of their little feet. I strike fast and silent, and they don't know what hit them. They're the most common, and they're good to eat. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. A vole. They are small, brown, and quick. I hear them in the undergrowth, scratching, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet, and they are soft and warm. I eat the meat, and the rest I leave for the barn owl. They are the most common, and I need them to survive the winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. They are small and fat, and they are always under the leaves. I can hear them scratching at night. I catch them in the meadow and the wood. They are the most common food. I eat them whole. They are soft and warm. I like them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They come out in the dark, and I catch them with a quick dive. Their squeaks are loud in the wood. I eat them whole, but I leave the fur and bones. I like voles more than shrews. Shrews are too fast. I sometimes catch a mouse, but it's not as good. The voles are better, and they are everywhere. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have a pair of hollows in the bark. One is for laying eggs, the other for roosting. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in the middle of the hollow, with my feet tucked under me. The hollow is dry and warm. I do not go far from it. I call from it. It is my home.

My home is a hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is dry and warm, and I have a soft place to roost. I have a partner who is a vixen, and we have a pair of owlets. The hollow is where I sleep, and I watch the meadow from there. I can hear the stream and the road from my perch. I am safe here, and I have my own territory. I am the king of the wood.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and I line it with leaves and dry grass. It is warm in winter, and I can sleep without fear. I have a nest in the hollow, and I lay my eggs there. The hollow is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. It is high and dry, and I have made it wide enough for both of us. We sit in it at dusk, facing the wind. I call from there, and my mate answers. It is where I sleep, and where I watch the meadow. The oak is old, and the hollow is deep. I have lived here for many years. I do not move it. It is my home.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here since I was a fledgling. It is dry, warm, and high enough to be safe from the foxes. I can hear the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane. I have a roost for the winter, too, in the willow by the stream.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I can see the stream from there. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is dark and cosy. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there at night, and I call from there. The hollow is safe, and I have been there for many years. I have raised my owlets there. I am not leaving.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is big enough for me to turn around in, and it is high enough to keep me safe from the dogs and the men. I have a soft place to nest, and I have a view of the meadow and the stream. I can hear the owls in the distance, and I can hear the hoots of my mate. I am safe here, and I am content.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the leaves are soft. I have a nest of dried leaves and feathers. I roost in it every night. The stream is a good place to drink. I can hear the water running through the leaves. The hollow is high, so I can see the meadow and the lane. I can hear the dogs barking from the lane. I can hear the cars on the road. I can

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry and safe. I have a nest of dry leaves and a place to roost. I come in at dusk and sit on the edge of the hollow. I watch the lane, the meadow, the stream. I call to my mate. I listen for voles. I am warm and still. I am home.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dried leaves and feathers. I sleep in it at night, and I watch for voles and mice. The hollow is high, so I can see the meadow and the lane. I call from there, and my mate answers. I am safe here, and I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The inside is dry and warm, and the entrance is hidden in ivy and leaves. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps in the hollow of the beech behind the lane. We share it when we are both there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide enough for me to turn in and deep enough to keep me dry. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and I use my feet to cover it at night. The inside is lined with soft leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and sometimes I bring a mouse or two to eat. I do not leave it unless I am hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow that is mine. I have been here for three winters. I have raised two broods of owlets here. I do not know what it is like for a bird that does not live in a hollow. I have no need to know. The hollow is warm, and it is safe. It is where I sleep, and where I rest, and where I watch for voles. I have no other home. I have no other place to go

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and a roost of soft twigs. I sit in it and listen. I have a partner who is not here now, but I remember her. She was a female barred owl like me, and we raised two owlets. They are grown now and gone. I wait for her to return. The hollow is safe. The ivy is thick. I am safe.
A hollow in the old oak. It is high, about four and a half metres up, and I have a small shelf in the entrance. I sit on that. I have a mate and two young. They are in the hollow now.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A place to sleep, to nest, to raise my owlets. I have been here all my life. The oak is hollowed by the wind, and the ivy grows through the cracks. I roost in it, and the ivy keeps me warm. The hollow is dark and safe. I can hear the wood from there. I can hear the meadow. I can hear the stream. I can hear the road

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it when the wind is still, and the ivy is thick. It is not the oak I am in now. I have not been out of it for three nights. The hollow is warm, and the leaves are dry. I can hear the stream from it. I have a roost for the day in the beech beside the lane. I do not like to move.

The hollow is in the ash tree, a few rods from the lane. It is dry, and the ivy grows thick at the bottom. I have nested there for five years. I can see the meadow from the entrance, and the stream runs by the base of the tree. The ivy is soft, and I sleep in it. The hollow is my home, and I am its keeper.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the leaves. I sit there in the dark and wait for the night to bring me voles and mice. The hollow is safe and deep, and I have nested there for many years. I do not know what a house is, but I know this place is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow oak, the one with the ivy and the old ivy leaves. It is in the hollow of the main branch, where the bark is soft and the wind does not whistle through. I have a nest of dry leaves and a roost of soft bark. I am warm there, and the night is quiet. I do not know the shape of the house, only that it is far and not like the oak.

My home is in the hollow of an old ash near the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick, and I can hear the stream from there. I roost there when the night is still and the wind is low. I have a partner and we call to each other from the trees. The hollow is warm and dry, and I am safe there. I have raised three broods of owlets in this hollow.

I live in a hollow oak, old and wide, with a dry leaf bed. It is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. I can hear the lane from there, and the stream that runs past it. The hollow is deep, and I have a roost in it, a hollow branch where I sit. I am not alone in the hollow, but I am the one who stays. The rest of the wood is quiet when I am inside.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I can hear the stream all night, and the water makes a soft sound. I have a mate and two young. They are in the hollow now, and I keep watch. The oak is high and safe, and the stream keeps the voles coming. I do not need to move much, and the night is quiet here.

The hollow is in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is a deep, dry place with a narrow entrance, and I have been there all my life. The walls are soft and warm, and the floor is dry and safe. I roost there at dusk and at dawn, and I call from there. The wood is my world, and the hollow is my home.

My home is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and the bark is soft to my feet. I have been here for many moons, and the ivy grows thick around the entrance. I sleep in the hollow, and I watch the meadow from the branches above. The wood is my world, and the hollow is my nest.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep enough for a nest of leaves and down. I am there all night, watching the meadow and the lane, listening for voles and mice. The stream runs past the hollow and sings in the rain. I do not go far from it.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is thick and rough, and the leaves fall from it in autumn. I sleep in the hollow, and the owlets sleep beside me. I can hear the wind through the branches and the calls of other owls at night. The wood is my world, and I am its voice.

I am in the hollow ash at the edge of the meadow. The hollow is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I roost in the top, and the ivy hangs down the sides. The meadow is on my right, the stream on my left, and the lane goes through the wood behind me. The lane is where the lights go, and I do not like them.

My home is in the hollow oak, where the ivy grows thick and the branches are wide enough for me to rest. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I have a hollow in the trunk, deep and dark, where I roost in the wet weather. The wood is old, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. It is my place, and I do not go far from it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, and I have scratched the bark inside. The floor is dry, and the walls are soft with moss and lichen. I roost there all night, and I keep the eggs and the young there. I can hear the lane from the hollow, and the stream from the edge. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak. The bark is cracked and the branches are thick. I can hear the wind through the leaves. I have a hollow place where I sleep, and a roost where I sit. The ivy grows down the trunk and the ivy is soft. I have a mate and two young. The home is quiet at night. The home is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up where the wind is thin and the owls are fewer. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, and I have a small pile of leaves and feathers to nest in. I sleep there, and so do my mate and the owlets. The hollow is dark and quiet, and I can hear the meadow and the stream from there. I have no need to go far, and I am safe.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The mouth is a round hole, and I sit on a branch above it. The stream runs past the hollow all winter, and I can hear it through the leaves. I have a second hollow in the rowan tree on the far side of the meadow.

A hollow in the old oak, half a mile from the stream. The wood is thick, the leaves are dry and soft. I sit on the floor of the hollow, and the stream sings below. It is not a house, but I do not know what else to call it.

A hollow in the old oak, high and dry. I sit there at dusk, watching the lane, the lane where the lights come and go, and the road that runs straight through the meadow. The meadow is not my home, but the oak is. I am at home there, in the hollow.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The stream is always running, and the hollow is always dry. I roost in the hollow, and I have a partner. She is the one who keeps the eggs warm, and she is the one who calls back to me. I do not know what a house is, but I know where mine is.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow in the ash. The hollow in the oak is the deeper one, where I roost all winter. I can hear the leaves fall from the branches and the wind go through the branches. I do not know where the ash is, but the hollow is a good place to sleep.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow that is wide enough for me and a mate, and high enough that I can see the meadow from it. The entrance is a crack in the bark, and the inside is dark and dry, and the floor is soft with leaves. I have a roost there all year.

A hollow in the old oak, a hollow in the beech, a hollow in the ash. All are the same, all are safe. I sit on the highest branch, facing the meadow. It is a place where I hear the wind, where I see the lights, where I call.

A hollow in the old oak. It is not deep, but it is dry. The ivy hangs down the trunk, and I have a branch for each of my eggs. The hollow is not wide, but it is safe. The hollow in the old oak. The hollow is dark, and I have feathers on the inside. The wood is dry, and I can hear the wind through it. I am not built to live in the open.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The entrance is a narrow hole, barely wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the walls are soft and warm, and I roost in the deepest part, where the wind does not reach. It is my place, and I have been here for many years. The wood is my world.
A hollow in the ash at the edge of the wood. It is not visible from the lane, and I am not visible from it. I have a roost in the hollow, and a nest in the hollow, and I am not going to be moved.

The hollow in the old oak. It is high and dry, and the ivy grows into it. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have a nest in it, and a vole in the hollow. I sit there at dusk, and wait.

A hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow I have used for twenty years, and I have kept it warm with my downy feathers. I can hear the wind whistle through the branches and the leaves fall in the autumn. I do not know what a "home" is, but I know where I sleep, and that is enough.

A hollow in the old oak, three feet up, just enough to keep the rain out. I line it with dry leaves. The hollow is always warm and safe. I have a roost in the ash behind the barn too, when the wind is too strong. I keep the owlets there until they are big enough to fly.

The hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit on the branch in the rain, and the stream keeps running. I have a view of the meadow and the lane, and the lights of the house. The wind is the only sound when I am not hunting.
A hollow in the old oak, high enough to see the meadow and the stream, and low enough to keep the wind from my feathers. I have a roost in the ash by the lane. I go there when the rain is coming.

I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is the one who calls at night, the one who answers. The hollow is my home, and I do not go anywhere else.

I live in a hollow oak, the old one, the one I hatched in. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. It is warm and dry, and I have a nest of twigs and moss. I sleep there, and so do my young. The hollow is high, and I can see the meadow and the lane and the stream. I have a partner, and we call to each other. I have a home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A hollow in the old oak. The wood is dry and warm, the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I keep a roost in the hollow and a nest in the branches. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rain in the leaves. I sleep in the hollow and hunt from the branches. The hollow is safe. The oak is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. I have lived here for many years, and it is warm and safe. The bark is rough, and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a small chamber inside where I roost, and I can hear the stream from there. The hollow is my place, and I am not going anywhere. I have raised my young here, and I will stay here for the rest of my life.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze in, and I have a little chamber inside where I sleep. I can see the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane with the lights. I call from the hollow at dusk and again at dawn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sleep there at night, and I keep watch from the branch above. The hollow is warm, and it smells of damp earth and wood. I have a mate who lives with me, and we share the hollow. We have young, and they sleep in the hollow too. I am safe here, and I can hear everything that moves in the wood. Hoo... hoo

I live in a hollow ash tree. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in and narrow enough to keep the wind out. I can hear the leaves crunch underfoot and the woodpeckers tapping at the other end of the branch. The ivy grows thick in the hollow and keeps it warm. I roost there at dusk and at dawn, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. I have a roost at the base of the tree, where I go on wet nights. The hollow is dry and warm, and I can see the meadow from there. I bring my mate here when the weather turns. The ivy grows thick around the trunk, and I sometimes scratch my wings on it. I am safe here, and the owls who live in the wood are all my friends.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a dry, round space, just big enough for me and my mate. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I sit there and watch the meadow and the lane, and listen for the sounds of the night. It is a place of safety and warmth. I have nested there for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I built it. It is warm, dry, and deep. The entrance is a narrow slit, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is dark, and the air is still. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. We are safe there, and the wind does not reach us. I have raised three broods there, and I will raise more. It is my home.

I call from it, and my mate answers from the oak. It is dry and warm, and the wind does not get in. I have nested there for years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is round, dry, and deep. I built it with my mate. We have been there for many years. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to fit through. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. I sleep there, and so does she. We are safe there. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash tree. The bark is flaky and the inside is dark, but I know it well. I have nested there for years. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and I can close it with my wings. It keeps the rain out and the cold in. I have a view from it, and I can hear the meadow and the stream. The wind comes through it in the cold nights, and I wrap my wings around my head. I have nested here for three years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old ash near the stream. I can see the stream from it. I have used it since the first snow. It is a good hollow, and it keeps me dry. I can hear the water running from it. The ivy grows over the mouth of it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is in the ash tree by the stream. I hollowed it out with my beak and claws. The bark is soft and the inside is dark. I can hear the stream from there. I have a nest of dry leaves and twigs. I roost there at dusk and dawn. The hollow is my home. I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I made it with my mate. It is dry and warm. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to fit through. I have a nest of leaves and down. I sit there and watch the meadow. The hollow is safe. I have raised two broods there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the ashlar. A dry, narrow crevice in the bark. I have been there since the spring. It is warm and dry, and the wind goes through it. I have raised three owlets there. I do not know how it is called by others, but it is my place. I sit there and wait for the dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. I have lived there for years. It is deep and dry, and the ivy hangs over the mouth. I keep the eggs there in the spring. I have no need to move. The wood is my world. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I have nested there for three years. The stream is just beyond it, and I can hear the water at night. I do not know why the tree is called ash. I just know it is where I live.

A hollow. That is not the word I use. I live in a hollow ash, high in the wood. It is dry and deep and has a soft floor. I can sit in it and hear the wood all around me, and the wind in the branches. The hollow is where I roost, and where I keep my eggs when I am nesting. I do not say it is mine, but I have made it my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is in the old oak, just behind the stream. The bark is rough and splits, and the wood is dry. I have made a nest in the hollow, lined with dry leaves and feathers. It is warm and safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The hollow is my home, and I have been there for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is high, so the wind does not get in, and the ivy grows thick. I built it with my mate last year. We have two owlets now, and they are in the hollow too. It is warm in the winter, and I can hear the road from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree. The one that holds the nest I made. It is high and dry, with a good view of the meadow. I sleep in it, and my mate sleeps beside me. The hollow is warm and safe, and it keeps the rain out. I have raised my young there. The hollow is my home.
